title: Correcting or Continuing?What On-Policy Distillation Learns from Student Errors

paper.title: Correcting or Continuing? What On-Policy Distillation Learns from Student Errors
paper.abstract: Abstract On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own rollouts under a frozen teacher, mitigating the distribution mismatch of off-policy supervision. While prior work has primarily trained on problems a student can largely solve, we ask whether OPD can improve a student when training is restricted to problems it currently fails. We evaluate five representative OPD mechanisms with Qwen-3 and Phi-4 models under a unified competition-mathematics protocol. We find that OPD does not improve accuracy on this hard subset, with most mechanisms instead degrading performance despite continued decreases in training KL divergence. All eight configurations show a decline, and the two-sided sign test gives p = 0.0078 p=0.0078 . In contrast, the same pipeline improves accuracy by 4.6 percentage points when training is not concentrated on failures, showing that the failure is conditional on the training regime rather than systematic. These findings suggest that OPD is effective when supervision is dominated by correct student prefixes, but can reinforce existing errors when training is concentrated on problems the student currently fails. 1 1 1 Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Correcting-or-Continuing-D74D/ .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Knowledge distillation aims to train a student model to imitate a stronger teacher model ( Hinton et al., 2015 ) . In on-policy distillation (OPD), the student generates its own outputs for a given task, and token-level supervision is computed from the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between the teacher and student logits ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) . This differs from earlier approaches that distill from a fixed corpus of teacher-generated samples rather than from the student’s own rollouts ( Kim and Rush, 2016 ) . On-policy distillation has recently been proposed as an alternative to reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for training small reasoning models ( Lu and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025 ; Ko et al., 2025 ; Shao et al., 2024 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ) . Figure 1: Closer to the teacher does not imply more correct. When the student’s prefix y < t y_{<t} already contains an error, on-policy distillation drives p S p_{S} toward p T ( ⋅ ∣ x , y < t ) p_{T}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t}) , reducing KL divergence yet failing to improve accuracy relative to the frozen student. Reported successes share a common regime in which supervision is dominated by correct student prefixes, either because the student is a tuned model or because much of the training distribution lies within its existing capabilities. We instead ask whether OPD can improve a student when training is restricted to problems it currently fails to solve, so that supervision is dominated by incorrect prefixes, as shown in Figure 1 . Therefore, we evaluate five mechanisms under a unified experimental protocol: a trained prompt rewriter, a soft-prefix encoder, a residual-stream offset, a per-token cross-attention steering vector, and full fine-tuning. Furthermore, we consider both forward and reverse KL objectives, as well as direct imitation. Our contributions are as follows: • Characterizing when improvement remains possible. We show that further gains are concentrated on problems the student currently fails to solve, suggesting that the remaining gap is primarily informational rather than a consequence of limited model capacity. • Establishing a robust negative result. Across five mechanisms, OPD fails to improve and often degrades accuracy, consistently across implementations with a sign test reaching p = 0.0078 p=0.0078 . • Identifying a conditional failure regime. The same pipeline significantly improves a weaker student on an easier benchmark ( p = 9.5 × 10 − 4 p=9.5\times 10^{-4} ), demonstrating that the negative result depends on the student and task regime rather than the training pipeline itself. • Tracing the failure. Our analyses provide evidence that supervision from incorrect prefixes can reinforce existing errors, while direct imitation of reference solutions does not recover the lost performance. We further identify three evaluation artifacts that can produce spurious positive results in this setting. Our findings suggest that OPD is effective when applied to a student whose rollouts are broadly correct, but can fail when supervision is concentrated on the narrow set of problems where the student already makes mistakes. This distinction becomes critical when applying OPD to already capable models.

sections.heading: 3.1 The Elicitation Ceiling
sections.text: We first quantify how much external supervision could improve the student in principle. We define the elicitation ratio as η acc = Acc method − Acc base Acc priv − Acc base , \eta_{\mathrm{acc}}=\frac{\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{method}}-\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{base}}}{\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{priv}}-\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{base}}}, (3) where Acc priv \mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{priv}} is the accuracy obtained when the frozen student is provided with the full worked reference solution in context. We use the worked solution rather than an answer-only string because the former provides the information required to solve the problem, whereas the latter primarily measures answer copying. The denominator therefore represents the improvement available through direct access to the reference solution. Because every mechanism in Section 3.2 decreases rather than improves accuracy, η acc \eta_{\mathrm{acc}} is negative for all methods. More importantly, none of the methods recovers a positive fraction of the available elicitation ceiling. On 800 problems sampled from the training distribution, evaluated with thinking enabled and a 16k-token budget, the student solves 89.6% without external supervision. As shown in Table 1 , 684 problems are therefore already solved by the student and provide no accuracy headroom. The remaining 116 problems contain nearly all of the available headroom: providing the reference solution increases accuracy by 26.9 percentage points, with a 95% confidence interval of 21.3–33.0 percentage points. On the hardest bucket, the corresponding gain reaches 50 percentage points, compared with only 3.9 percentage points overall. The substantial improvement from reference-conditioned supervision on the hardest problems indicates that the student retains sufficient capacity to solve these problems when provided with the relevant information. The remaining failure of OPD therefore points to a gap in eliciting existing capability rather than a lack of model capacity. A second, independent measurement provides consistent evidence. Under a leakage-free constraint, clean prompt rewriting attains an accuracy ceiling of only about two percentage points. Furthermore, the teacher-likelihood reward used to select rewrites is negatively correlated with answer correctness, yielding a Spearman correlation of ρ = − 0.41 \rho=-0.41 . This suggests that higher teacher likelihood does not reliably identify correct rewrites. Full details are provided in Appendix B . We therefore focus our OPD experiments on a hard subset of 1,034 problems selected from 8,000 candidates. Each selected problem has a base accuracy of at most 0.75. sections.heading: 3.2 subIsolation Study Across Mechanisms
sections.text: Setup. We distill Qwen3-1.7B-Instruct using a frozen Qwen3-4B-Instruct teacher ( Yang et al., 2025 ) on the 904-problem hard subset. We vary the distillation mechanism, KL direction, and training implementation, comparing our in-house implementation with the standard TRL trainer. Figure 2 reports the change in AIME24 ( Zhang and Math-AI, 2024 ) pass@1 accuracy relative to the untouched student. We use 30 problems, grade boxed answers with a math verifier, and allow up to 16k generated tokens. A second, independently implemented codebase evaluates activation-level steering with the frozen student. It uses three mechanisms: a soft prefix, a residual-stream offset, and a per-token steering vector derived from cross-attention over the problem’s hidden states. The corresponding results are reported in Table 2 . Appendix C provides implementation details for all five mechanisms, Appendix B reports the trained prompt-rewriter results, and Appendix F provides the complete hyperparameter and hardware configuration. Results. All evaluated configurations yield non-positive accuracy changes. Varying model capacity, KL direction, gating and warm-up, teacher scale, or training framework does not reverse this direction. Meanwhile, token-level KL decreases throughout training even when held-out accuracy declines. We assess the consistency of this effect using a two-sided sign test ( Dixon and Mood, 1946 ) under a symmetric null of zero effect. To test whether the observed failure reflects a systematic issue in our implementation, we apply the same TRL reverse-KL pipeline to settings in which OPD has previously been shown to improve performance. Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, distilled from Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct ( Qwen et al., 2025 ) on GSM8K prompts ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) , improves from 43.6% to 48.2% accuracy over 1,319 problems, corresponding to a statistically significant gain at p = 9.5 × 10 − 4 p=9.5\times 10^{-4} . Phi-4-mini-instruct ( Abouelenin et al., 2025 ) , distilled from a same-size Phi-4-mini-reasoning teacher ( Xu et al., 2025 ) , improves from 67% to 74% on MATH-500 ( Lightman et al., 2023 ) . This second control is not competence-matched and therefore serves only as an additional positive control. Full details are provided in Appendix D . These positive controls provide evidence against a general defect in the training pipeline. However, because they vary student capability, benchmark difficulty, and model family simultaneously, they do not isolate the factor responsible for the observed difference.

sections.heading: 3.3 Failure Mode: Supervision on an Incorrect Prefix
sections.text: Our setting differs from those in which OPD has previously succeeded: the student is already capable, receives no supervised warm-up, and is trained only on problems it currently fails. This creates a failure mode inherent to the on-policy objective in Equation 1 . The KL supervision is computed on the student’s sampled prefix y < t y_{<t} . When this prefix contains an incorrect step, the teacher is conditioned on an already erroneous state rather than on the correct solution path. The resulting supervision therefore cannot directly correct the error that generated the prefix and may instead reinforce the student’s existing trajectory. Figure 2 is consistent with this mechanism: training KL decreases while held-out accuracy also declines. Stress test. We ask whether the failure is simply caused by the absence of a gold solution as an explicit anchor. Providing supervision directly from the reference solution does not resolve the problem. Row three of Table 2 decreases accuracy by 11.7% in a single run, which we interpret as evidence of direction rather than effect size given the seed variability above. A subsequent on-policy KL step recovers accuracy only to the untouched baseline. A related soft-prefix analysis offers further evidence. Across 94 problems, the learned prefixes are nearly collinear, with pairwise cosine similarities of 0.998–0.999, whereas the underlying problem representations yield only 0.78 and a single direction accounts for 70–73% of their variance. As the checkpoint corresponding to row three was not retained, these results constitute consistent rather than direct evidence. We therefore interpret the observed recovery as the removal of a self-induced deficit rather than the elicitation of new capability. Evaluation artifacts. Three artifacts can produce spurious positive results in this setting. Permissive regex matching can overstate gains: an apparent 11.7% improvement fell to 0.8% after requiring a verified boxed answer. An insufficient generation budget can truncate reasoning and drive both baseline and treatment accuracy to 0, producing a misleading null result. Finally, answer leakage through unaudited rewrites can inflate apparent gains by 10–20 %. Appendix E provides details.

sections.heading: 4 Conclusion
sections.text: Across five mechanisms and three training objectives, OPD does not reliably improve a student when training is restricted to problems it currently fails. The negative direction is consistent across eight configurations, while a positive control improves accuracy by 4.6 percentage points under the same pipeline, indicating that the failure depends on the training regime rather than on an implementation defect. These results delineate the boundary of standard OPD: it is effective when supervision is dominated by correct student prefixes, but can reinforce existing errors when supervision is concentrated on incorrect prefixes. Future work should isolate student capability from task difficulty under matched conditions, test whether outcome-based reinforcement learning exhibits a similar failure mode, and develop objectives that correct erroneous prefixes rather than imitate the teacher on them.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Our findings highlight the potential risks of applying on-policy distillation without carefully assessing its effects on model capabilities. In particular, training primarily on problems that the student cannot solve may reinforce erroneous reasoning rather than improve accuracy, potentially propagating errors to downstream applications. However, our negative evidence is drawn from Qwen3, and is evaluated primarily on one hard-mathematics subset. Its transferability to other settings therefore remains unknown. AIME24 contains only thirty items, therefore we accordingly claim directional consistency rather than effect magnitude throughout. Furthermore, training and evaluating multiple distillation configurations incurs computational costs and associated environmental impacts, although we do not quantify energy consumption in this work. These considerations underscore the importance of evaluating both task-level performance and error patterns before deploying models trained with on-policy distillation.

sections.heading: Ethical Considerations
sections.text: The findings of this work raise broader questions about responsibility in the development and evaluation of AI systems. Distillation can make a model appear to be learning from a more capable teacher, yet improvements in optimization metrics do not necessarily translate into greater practical competence. Treating such metrics as proxies for capability may create misplaced confidence in models whose errors remain unresolved. This is particularly consequential in settings where model outputs inform human judgments or decisions, as errors may be accepted or propagated when users overestimate a system’s reliability. Our work highlights the importance of critically examining what training procedures actually teach models, rather than assuming that successful optimization implies meaningful capability gains. We propose that our results will motivate greater scrutiny of the assumptions underlying model evaluation and deployment.

sections.heading: Appendix A Related Work
sections.text: On-policy distillation and related generalized distillation objectives train a student on its own rollouts under the supervision of a frozen teacher ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2024 ; Ko et al., 2024 ; Ko et al., 2025 ) . Existing studies typically initialize the student from a base or weakly tuned model that has already received supervised warm-up ( Lu and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2024 ) . Recent work has identified several pathologies of on-policy supervision, including degraded supervision as the student’s rollouts diverge from the teacher’s distribution ( Xie et al., 2026 ) and unreliable guidance when a generated prefix leaves the teacher’s support ( Fu et al., 2026 ) . These studies primarily diagnose such failures and propose modifications to the objective. In contrast, we investigate under what conditions the standard objective remains effective, evaluating multiple distillation mechanisms and validating our findings with both a positive control and a stress test. Several recent extensions modify the standard distillation objective or its information available to the teacher. Reward-weighted generalizations can allow a student to surpass its teacher ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . Our results concern the standard KL-based and imitation objectives on a single challenging domain and therefore do not directly address such reward-weighted formulations. Privileged self-distillation instead conditions the teacher on the reference solution ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) . We study the standard teacher-student setting without privileged information and consider reference-conditioned supervision only as a stress test. Our experiments also include prompt rewriting as discrete forms of intervention ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Kong et al., 2024 ) . Our results highlight the need to examine rewriters for answer leakage when evaluating their effectiveness. Finally, our identified failure mode arises from supervision computed over the student’s own sampled tokens, whereas reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards typically provides supervision from the final outcome ( Shao et al., 2024 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ) . Whether outcome-based reinforcement learning exhibits an analogous failure mode remains an open question, as does the broader question of whether such training induces genuinely new reasoning capabilities or primarily reinforces capabilities already present in the model’s distribution ( Yue et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) .

What On-Policy Distillation Learns from Student Errors Shuo Yang Zheyu Zhang Mahito Sugiyama Gjergji Kasneci Email: shuo.yang@tum.de, zheyu.zhang@tum.de, mahito@nii.ac.jp, gjergji.kasneci@tum.de Affiliation: Technical University of Munich Affiliation: National Institute of Informatics Affiliation: Munich Center for Machine Learning Abstract On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own rollouts under a frozen teacher, mitigating the distribution mismatch of off-policy supervision. While prior work has primarily trained on problems a student can largely solve, we ask whether OPD can improve a student when training is restricted to problems it currently fails. We evaluate five representative OPD mechanisms with Qwen-3 and Phi-4 models under a unified competition-mathematics protocol. We find that OPD does not improve accuracy on this hard subset, with most mechanisms instead degrading performance despite continued decreases in training KL divergence. All eight configurations show a decline, and the two-sided sign test gives p = 0.0078 p=0.0078 . In contrast, the same pipeline improves accuracy by 4.6 percentage points when training is not concentrated on failures, showing that the failure is conditional on the training regime rather than systematic. These findings suggest that OPD is effective when supervision is dominated by correct student prefixes, but can reinforce existing errors when training is concentrated on problems the student currently fails. 1 1 1 Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Correcting-or-Continuing-D74D/ . 1 Introduction Knowledge distillation aims to train a student model to imitate a stronger teacher model ( Hinton et al., 2015 ) . In on-policy distillation (OPD), the student generates its own outputs for a given task, and token-level supervision is computed from the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between the teacher and student logits ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) . This differs from earlier approaches that distill from a fixed corpus of teacher-generated samples rather than from the student’s own rollouts ( Kim and Rush, 2016 ) . On-policy distillation has recently been proposed as an alternative to reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for training small reasoning models ( Lu and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025 ; Ko et al., 2025 ; Shao et al., 2024 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ) . Figure 1: Closer to the teacher does not imply more correct. When the student’s prefix y < t y_{<t} already contains an error, on-policy distillation drives p S p_{S} toward p T ( ⋅ ∣ x , y < t ) p_{T}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t}) , reducing KL divergence yet failing to improve accuracy relative to the frozen student. Reported successes share a common regime in which supervision is dominated by correct student prefixes, either because the student is a tuned model or because much of the training distribution lies within its existing capabilities. We instead ask whether OPD can improve a student when training is restricted to problems it currently fails to solve, so that supervision is dominated by incorrect prefixes, as shown in Figure 1 . Therefore, we evaluate five mechanisms under a unified experimental protocol: a trained prompt rewriter, a soft-prefix encoder, a residual-stream offset, a per-token cross-attention steering vector, and full fine-tuning. Furthermore, we consider both forward and reverse KL objectives, as well as direct imitation. Our contributions are as follows: • Characterizing when improvement remains possible. We show that further gains are concentrated on problems the student currently fails to solve, suggesting that the remaining gap is primarily informational rather than a consequence of limited model capacity. • Establishing a robust negative result. Across five mechanisms, OPD fails to improve and often degrades accuracy, consistently across implementations with a sign test reaching p = 0.0078 p=0.0078 . • Identifying a conditional failure regime. The same pipeline significantly improves a weaker student on an easier benchmark ( p = 9.5 × 10 − 4 p=9.5\times 10^{-4} ), demonstrating that the negative result depends on the student and task regime rather than the training pipeline itself. • Tracing the failure. Our analyses provide evidence that supervision from incorrect prefixes can reinforce existing errors, while direct imitation of reference solutions does not recover the lost performance. We further identify three evaluation artifacts that can produce spurious positive results in this setting. Our findings suggest that OPD is effective when applied to a student whose rollouts are broadly correct, but can fail when supervision is concentrated on the narrow set of problems where the student already makes mistakes. This distinction becomes critical when applying OPD to already capable models. 2 Problem Setup We formulate reverse-KL on-policy distillation as minimizing the KL divergence from the student distribution to the teacher distribution along trajectories sampled from the student: 𝔼 x , y ∼ p S ( ⋅ | x ) ∑ t KL ( p S ( ⋅ | x , y < t ) ∥ p T ( ⋅ | x , y < t ) ) . \mathbb{E}_{x,y\sim p_{S}(\cdot|x)}\sum_{t}\mathrm{KL}(p_{S}(\cdot|x,y_{<t})\|p_{T}(\cdot|x,y_{<t})). The denominator therefore represents the improvement available through direct access to the reference solution. Because every mechanism in Section 3.2 decreases rather than improves accuracy, η acc \eta_{\mathrm{acc}} is negative for all methods. On the hardest bucket, the corresponding gain reaches 50 percentage points, compared with only 3.9 percentage points overall. The substantial improvement from reference-conditioned supervision on the hardest problems indicates that the student retains sufficient capacity to solve these problems when provided with the relevant information. The remaining failure of OPD therefore points to a gap in eliciting existing capability rather than a lack of model capacity. A second, independent measurement provides consistent evidence. To test whether the observed failure reflects a systematic issue in our implementation, we apply the same TRL reverse-KL pipeline to settings in which OPD has previously been shown to improve performance. Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, distilled from Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct ( Qwen et al., 2025 ) on GSM8K prompts ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) , improves from 43.6% to 48.2% accuracy over 1,319 problems, corresponding to a statistically significant gain at p = 9.5 × 10 − 4 p=9.5\times 10^{-4} . This second control is not competence-matched and therefore serves only as an additional positive control. Full details are provided in Appendix D . These positive controls provide evidence against a general defect in the training pipeline. However, because they vary student capability, benchmark difficulty, and model family simultaneously, they do not isolate the factor responsible for the observed difference. 3.3 Failure Mode: Supervision on an Incorrect Prefix Our setting differs from those in which OPD has previously succeeded: the student is already capable, receives no supervised warm-up, and is trained only on problems it currently fails. This creates a failure mode inherent to the on-policy objective in Equation 1 . The KL supervision is computed on the student’s sampled prefix y < t y_{<t} . When this prefix contains an incorrect step, the teacher is conditioned on an already erroneous state rather than on the correct solution path. The resulting supervision therefore cannot directly correct the error that generated the prefix and may instead reinforce the student’s existing trajectory. Figure 2 is consistent with this mechanism: training KL decreases while held-out accuracy also declines. Stress test. We ask whether the failure is simply caused by the absence of a gold solution as an explicit anchor. Providing supervision directly from the reference solution does not resolve the problem. Row three of Table 2 decreases accuracy by 11.7% in a single run, which we interpret as evidence of direction rather than effect size given the seed variability above. A subsequent on-policy KL step recovers accuracy only to the untouched baseline. A related soft-prefix analysis offers further evidence. Across 94 problems, the learned prefixes are nearly collinear, with pairwise cosine similarities of 0.998–0.999, whereas the underlying problem representations yield only 0.78 and a single direction accounts for 70–73% of their variance. As the checkpoint corresponding to row three was not retained, these results constitute consistent rather than direct evidence. We therefore interpret the observed recovery as the removal of a self-induced deficit rather than the elicitation of new capability. Evaluation artifacts. Three artifacts can produce spurious positive results in this setting. Permissive regex matching can overstate gains: an apparent 11.7% improvement fell to 0.8% after requiring a verified boxed answer. An insufficient generation budget can truncate reasoning and drive both baseline and treatment accuracy to 0, producing a misleading null result. Finally, answer leakage through unaudited rewrites can inflate apparent gains by 10–20 %. Appendix E provides details. 4 Conclusion Across five mechanisms and three training objectives, OPD does not reliably improve a student when training is restricted to problems it currently fails. The negative direction is consistent across eight configurations, while a positive control improves accuracy by 4.6 percentage points under the same pipeline, indicating that the failure depends on the training regime rather than on an implementation defect. These results delineate the boundary of standard OPD: it is effective when supervision is dominated by correct student prefixes, but can reinforce existing errors when supervision is concentrated on incorrect prefixes. Future work should isolate student capability from task difficulty under matched conditions, test whether outcome-based reinforcement learning exhibits a similar failure mode, and develop objectives that correct erroneous prefixes rather than imitate the teacher on them. Limitations Our findings highlight the potential risks of applying on-policy distillation without carefully assessing its effects on model capabilities. In particular, training primarily on problems that the student cannot solve may reinforce erroneous reasoning rather than improve accuracy, potentially propagating errors to downstream applications. However, our negative evidence is drawn from Qwen3, and is evaluated primarily on one hard-mathematics subset. Its transferability to other settings therefore remains unknown. AIME24 contains only thirty items, therefore we accordingly claim directional consistency rather than effect magnitude throughout. Furthermore, training and evaluating multiple distillation configurations incurs computational costs and associated environmental impacts, although we do not quantify energy consumption in this work. These considerations underscore the importance of evaluating both task-level performance and error patterns before deploying models trained with on-policy distillation. Ethical Considerations The findings of this work raise broader questions about responsibility in the development and evaluation of AI systems. Distillation can make a model appear to be learning from a more capable teacher, yet improvements in optimization metrics do not necessarily translate into greater practical competence. Treating such metrics as proxies for capability may create misplaced confidence in models whose errors remain unresolved. This is particularly consequential in settings where model outputs inform human judgments or decisions, as errors may be accepted or propagated when users overestimate a system’s reliability. Our work highlights the importance of critically examining what training procedures actually teach models, rather than assuming that successful optimization implies meaningful capability gains. Appendix A Related Work On-policy distillation and related generalized distillation objectives train a student on its own rollouts under the supervision of a frozen teacher ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2024 ; Ko et al., 2024 ; Ko et al., 2025 ) . Existing studies typically initialize the student from a base or weakly tuned model that has already received supervised warm-up ( Lu and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2024 ) . Recent work has identified several pathologies of on-policy supervision, including degraded supervision as the student’s rollouts diverge from the teacher’s distribution ( Xie et al., 2026 ) and unreliable guidance when a generated prefix leaves the teacher’s support ( Fu et al., 2026 ) . These studies primarily diagnose such failures and propose modifications to the objective. In contrast, we investigate under what conditions the standard objective remains effective, evaluating multiple distillation mechanisms and validating our findings with both a positive control and a stress test. Several recent extensions modify the standard distillation objective or its information available to the teacher. Reward-weighted generalizations can allow a student to surpass its teacher ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . Our results concern the standard KL-based and imitation objectives on a single challenging domain and therefore do not directly address such reward-weighted formulations. Privileged self-distillation instead conditions the teacher on the reference solution ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) . We study the standard teacher-student setting without privileged information and consider reference-conditioned supervision only as a stress test. Our experiments also include prompt rewriting as discrete forms of intervention ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Kong et al., 2024 ) . Our results highlight the need to examine rewriters for answer leakage when evaluating their effectiveness. Finally, our identified failure mode arises from supervision computed over the student’s own sampled tokens, whereas reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards typically provides supervision from the final outcome ( Shao et al., 2024 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ) . Whether outcome-based reinforcement learning exhibits an analogous failure mode remains an open question, as does the broader question of whether such training induces genuinely new reasoning capabilities or primarily reinforces capabilities already present in the model’s distribution ( Yue et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) .
